text_2: Within each half of the villa, every room is given one stone of its own, from veined green marble in the kitchen and formal living to a backlit marble library in the family room, raw fractured stone in the powder room, and green onyx in an ensuite. What holds them together never changes – oak, plaster, a bronze profile, a line of light – but no two rooms repeat, so the house reads as a sequence of authored spaces rather than one specification stretched thin.

The arch, lifted from the villa’s architecture, becomes the grammar of the interior, returning as illuminated niches in the formal living, as an oval ring chandelier that answers it in plan, as bronze arcs across the fluted-glass screens between living and dining, and as the oval table beneath the pendants. Threaded through all of it is a single line of light, a glowing seam that begins in the marble floor at the threshold, climbs the inner edge of the spiral stair and lands on the first-floor gallery, stitching the two floors and the two moods of the house together.
text_3: For all the depth of its materials, the villa is quieter than it looks – dark yet warm downstairs, bright yet grounded upstairs, formal in plan but relaxed in the way it is lived. The result is not a house that merely accommodates its programme, but a complete home shaped by two kinds of light, one line of bronze, and the discipline of giving every room its own stone.
name: Lumen
text_1: Lumen is a private family villa set on the lagoons of Jumeirah Islands, modest in footprint but carrying the programme of a far larger house. The brief asked for two homes in one: a ground floor built to host, a kitchen worth cooking in front of guests and a dining room for ten; and an upper floor given entirely to family life, with every bedroom opening onto the lagoon.

The house is drawn in two moods that answer the hours of the day. Downstairs is the evening house, where fumed oak, polished grey-brown marble and deep green stone are lit low and warm, so that formal dinners and quiet nights at home share the same enveloping calm. Upstairs is the morning house, in which pale oak floors, soft plaster and light timber take over, and every bedroom opens onto the lagoon through sheer curtains that move with the water.
